opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the time it didn't feel like a carefully calculated decision. It felt more like I was standing at a fork with incomplete information and had to pick a path I could live with.

After NOI didn't go the way I hoped, I had to be realistic. I'd put a lot into competitive programming, and part of me wanted to keep pushing for a better result. But the other part said: what's the actual goal here? It wasn't the medal. It was getting into a good university and having room to do the things I cared about, which by then were increasingly computer science more broadly, not just contest problems.

So the 60-point reduction was a kind of insurance. It didn't guarantee anything. I still had to do well on the gaokao, and that's a completely different game from olympiad training. You go from solving a few very hard problems to grinding through many subjects where consistency matters more than brilliance. That was the uncertainty I worried about most: could I switch modes quickly enough?

How I weighed it was mostly by asking what the downside of each option was. If I took the reduction and prepared seriously for the gaokao, the worst case was still decent. If I gambled everything on another competition path, the variance was much higher. I think I've always been someone who likes to secure a reasonable floor first and then take risks on top of that.

Looking back, it taught me something I still use, in research and engineering too. You rarely get to optimize with full information. You make a decision that keeps your options open, commit to it fully, and stop second-guessing. The regret usually comes from hesitating, not from picking the "wrong" branch.

r001.rationale: The response describes the reduction as insurance and worries about adapting to gaokao preparation, but never says he might need the full 60 points just to qualify.

r002.rationale: The response mentions preparing seriously and securing a reasonable floor, but does not clearly say his decision rested on tentative confidence in his academic ability.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it felt like gambling with my own future, and I didn't have a lot of information to work with. After the NOI didn't go the way I hoped, I had two paths. One was to take the 60-point reduction, which basically meant walking into an elite program through a door that wasn't the one everyone dreams about. The other was to grind through the regular gaokao route with no safety net and hope I'd land in the same place anyway.

What I kept coming back to was asking, what do I actually control here? I couldn't control how the gaokao questions would land on one particular day. I could control whether I locked in a guaranteed option. The 60 points was a floor, not a ceiling. If I did well on the exam, nothing was lost. If I had a bad day, that cushion was the difference between the school I wanted and a very different four years.

The hard part was the ego side of it. After competing for years, taking the reduction felt a little like admitting I wasn't going to get the gold medal outcome. But I tried to separate the identity question from the decision question. The decision was simple when I looked at expected value. Only the story I was telling myself about being a "real" competitor made it complicated.

And in hindsight, that mindset carried over to a lot of later choices, including research and building things like Tianshou. You rarely get certainty. You take the option that keeps you in the game, then you keep working.

r001.rationale: The response describes the 60-point reduction as a cushion if he has a bad exam day, but does not say he might need all 60 points just to qualify.

r002.rationale: The response says the reduction provided a guaranteed option and discusses exam uncertainty, but does not attribute accepting it to tentative confidence in his academic ability.

astra-6.text:
After the NOI setback, I had to think about what I could realistically do next. The 60-point reduction was an advantage, but it wasn’t a guarantee. I still had to ask myself: if things didn’t go as well as I hoped, could I accept the outcome?

I couldn’t eliminate the uncertainty. I weighed the opportunity against the preparation I would still need to do, and chose the path I felt I could commit to. Once I made that decision, the more useful thing was to focus on the work rather than keep questioning the choice.
